cur:manuscripts-rossano-good-samaritan.summary: Beside the walled city of Jerusalem, the Good Samaritan — shown with Christ's features, golden halo and gold mantle — bends over the wounded man lying by the road, helped by an angel holding a bowl; then, leading the man on his donkey, he pays the innkeeper. The parable is read as an image of Christ himself coming to heal wounded humanity. Prophets below witness with their scrolls.
facts: Identifying the Samaritan with Christ follows an interpretation of the parable already common among early Church writers.
The angel assisting the Samaritan is not in the Gospel text; it underlines that the helper is divine.

cur:manuscripts-rabbula-christ-enthroned.summary: Under a gabled canopy framed by columns, Christ sits enthroned and blessing, holding a book, while four monks in dark habits stand around him, two of them presenting a book. The image is generally read as a dedication, the makers of the Gospel offering their work to Christ. Its simple, frontal composition contrasts with the crowded narrative pages that precede it.
facts: The Rabbula Gospels was completed in 586 and signed by the scribe Rabbula, about whom nothing else is known.
Recent scholarship has proposed that its miniatures may come from at least one other manuscript and were bound together with the text of 586 only in the 15th century.
cur:manuscripts-rabbula-christ-enthroned.notes: Commons gives fol. 14r; the Wikipedia list places 'Christ with four monks' on the same leaf as the Ascension (fol. 14a). Folio numbering varies between publications.

cur:manuscripts-otto-iii-prayer-book-dee.summary: In the upper register Christ stands frontally holding a book, while John the Baptist and the Virgin turn toward him in intercession; below, a bareheaded young layman in a gold-trimmed robe — the young king — stands in prayer between Saints Peter and Paul. The page sets the royal reader within the chain of heavenly intercession.
facts: Made between 984 and 991 for the private use of the young King Otto III, this is the only surviving prayer book of an Ottonian king; it is tiny (15 × 12 cm), written in gold on painted purple, with five full-page miniatures.
German Wikipedia identifies the upper scene as a Deesis and the lower figure as a young layman between Peter and Paul, generally taken to be Otto III.

getty:9148d3ac-44a4-4573-b54d-53f02f4854.summary: Inside an ornamental frame, Christ sits on a green mountaintop, raised above six disciples who stand symmetrically on either side and turn toward him. He holds a book in one hand and gestures with the other, as if answering a question, and like his apostles wears a Roman-style pallium. The painter drew the drapery in agitated spirals and zigzags that charge the balanced composition with energy.
facts: The Getty describes the leaf as coming from a Gospel book made about 1000, perhaps at Canterbury in England.
The museum notes that the artist emphasised Christ's role as teacher by placing him higher than his apostles, giving him more space and turning all of them toward him.
getty:9148d3ac-44a4-4573-b54d-53f02f4854.notes: The Getty does not tie the scene to a specific Gospel passage; the Sermon on the Mount is cited only as a theme. Much of the page around the miniature is blank and the leaf is irregularly cut.

princeton:19972.summary: The two hinged halves of this small bronze reliquary cross are shown one above the other. On the upper half a figure with outstretched arms, worn almost smooth, appears to be the crucified Christ; on the lower half the Virgin stands in a long robe with her hands raised in prayer. Worn on the breast, such crosses enclosed a relic between their two halves.
facts: Princeton records the cross as Middle Byzantine, from Ashdod in Palestine, 9th–11th century; it is only 5.8 cm high.
Pairing Christ on one leaf with the praying Virgin on the other is a common scheme of Middle Byzantine bronze reliquary crosses (type).
princeton:19972.notes: The figure of Christ is heavily worn; identification follows the museum title. The 'type' fact is general knowledge about such encolpia, not a statement about this object.
